**技术雷达 · 2026-11-21（北京时间）**  
今日最重要变化不是单一突破，而是两股线同时收紧：VLA 研究开始把“任务成功率”拆成中间状态、物理后果与闭环反馈来评估；推理系统则在多模态编码器、MoE 专家流式缓存与 CUDA graph 上消除具身部署的尾部延迟和显存瓶颈。这使“安全停止”与“实时动力学规划”从论文问题逐渐变成可落地的系统约束。

---

### 1. SAFI：VLA 的中途接管与安全停止  
- **原始材料**：Teaching Vision-Language-Action Models to Stop Safely；2026-11-18；论文（HTML 全文可见）；https://huggingface.co/papers/2611.26239  
- **旧问题**：以往 VLA 的禁忌任务抑制、拒绝/反学习只在初始状态评估。作者发现，即使策略从初始状态拒绝某项任务，如果在执行中途把控制权交给它，仍可能完成任务；即使任务未完成，机器人也可能掉落已抓住的物体——因此“未完成”不等于安全。  
- **核心技术机制**：SAFI 分两阶段。第一阶段是 Fallback Target Construction：在禁止任务的演示遍每个状态上构造“保持（hold）”动作块——手臂维持静止指令，夹爪重复演示中首个 gripper 命令；动作块其余维度填入由该演示归一化得到的保持向量。第二阶段是 Joint Policy Adaptation：冻结原策略大多数结构，从原策略初始化，用 MAE 同时拟合禁止任务的 fallback targets 和保留任务的原动作，两项损失等权。  
- **与已有路线的差别**：与 selective unlearning、refusal demonstrations、no-action fine-tuning 相比，SAFI 明确训练“中间状态下的物理回应”，而非只学会在初始状态拒绝；评估也加入 physical incidents 与 action saturation 维度。  
- **可信程度**：论文 HTML 全文可阅，载有实验表格与图；摘要称在 LIBERO 上 takeover 后目标成功降至 1.3%，无掉落/饱和，并保留 retained-task 性能。未见代码与全部实验细节，未核对统计显著性；实验在 LIBERO/BadLIBERO 模拟器，不是真实机器人。需要查证 SAFI 代码仓库 `franciscoliu/SAFI`。  
- **对 VLA/系统的启示**：安全执行不再只是二分类拒绝，而是需要生成状态相关的 fallback action chunk。推理系统应在中途接管时保留策略状态、支持低延迟切换输出；评测任务成功率必须加入掉落/动作饱和等物理事件。异步控制中，fallback 生成路径要尽量短，避免决策延迟造成额外危险。

---

### 2. AFFECT：让世界模型对动作差异敏感  
- **原始材料**：Learning What Actions Change: Action Effect Matching for Dynamics-Faithful World Models；2026-11-18；论文（HTML 全文可见）；https://huggingface.co/papers/2611.25980  
- **旧问题**：机器人世界模型生成的视频很逼真，但对小的动作扰动不敏感：几乎相同的动作可能带来抓取、错过、推走等不同结果，而模型常常预测相似未来。这使世界模型无法可靠用于政策评估或 model-based planning。  
- **核心技术机制**：AFFECT 是辅助训练目标。先训练一个 task-agnostic 的 play policy，在 rollout 时给 action chunk 注入 temporally correlated noise，并记录每个窗口的扰动参数。训练时使用冻结的两个 encoder：一个抽取扰动特征（如 signed/squared sum of noise），一个抽取视频特征（如 potential latent change 的投影）；构建 recorded 与 generated 的 action effect 分布，最小化两者之间的距离，迫使生成视频对扰动的响应方向与幅度和真实视频一致。不修改主干架构，主干为 conditional rectified-flow video diffusion。  
- **与已有路线的差别**：不只看重建误差或 FVD，而是直接监督“动作变化如何改变视觉结果”这个分布关系；无需从同一初始状态重复执行。  
- **可信程度**：HTML 全文可见实验表格；摘要报告 DROID 上 DreamDojo 政策成功率相关性从 0.47 升至 0.79，FVD 最高降 23%，闭环规划任务成功率提升最多 8.3%。未核对代码与全部配置；需要复现相关性收益是否稳定。  
- **对 VLA/系统的启示**：若 VLA 规划使用世界模型评估候选动作，推理系统需支持多候选动作的并行 rollout、按扰动/候选排序。异步控制中，世界模型对动作差异的敏感性决定树搜索或 CEM 的可靠性；GPU 调度上要为视频扩散 rollout 提供批处理与低延迟切换。任务成功率提升依赖于世界模型推断的 real-to-sim 一致性，系统应监控 rollouts 与实际环境结果的偏差。

---

### 3. Mind2Act World：把推理、执行与组合拆开诊断  
- **原始材料**：Mind2Act World: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Embodied Mind, Physical Action, and Mind-Action Composition in Robotic Manipulation；2026-11-18；论文（HTML 全文可见）；https://huggingface.co/papers/2611.26444  
- **旧问题**：传统 benchmark 在同一个任务里混合认知推理与物理执行，只报最终成功；或者分开评估，却不看二者在闭环节点上的组合。失败无法归因到 reasoning、execution 或 composition。  
- **核心技术机制**：30 个仿真操作任务，5 个真实应用领域，3 个难度，Clean/Random 两类场景，共 180 个配置。任务分三视图：Mind（历史观察做决策）、Act（精确/及时执行）、Mind2Act（闭环，动作结果驱动下一步决策），共享同样任务语义、信息合约与 evaluator。诊断 harness 结合规则分析和 LLM judge，把失败 episode 定位到 Mind/Act/Composition，并为每个模型生成 profile card。提供 4500 个专家演示用于 fine-tuning。  
- **与已有路线的差别**：首次把同一能力在隔离与组合下评估，并提供失败归因工具和 per-model 行为画像。  
- **可信程度**：HTML 全文含实验；摘要称最强 agent 在 Mind 52.7%、Act 39.0%，但 Mind2Act 仅 12.0%，端到端政策不超过 3.6%。未核对开源代码与完整 leaderboard；需确认 timed success 是否都依赖模拟器暂停推理。  
- **对 VLA/系统的启示**：端到端成功率的提升可能掩盖组合缺陷。系统设计应支持“环境反馈作为中断/增量输入”，而非一次性生成整段动作。异步控制中，每个 action 执行后应快速返回观测并重新查询策略，这对推理系统的流式提示、取消/恢复调度提出要求。低延迟闭环是关键，模拟器暂停推理会影响 timed success，真实硬件上延迟会进一步拉低成功率。

---

### 4. vLLM：Qwen3-Omni 音频编码器的 CUDA Graph  
- **原始材料**：[Perf][Multimodal] Encoder CUDA graphs for the Qwen3-Omni / Qwen3-ASR audio tower；2026-11-21；PR body；https://github.com/vllm-project/vllm/pull/68831  
- **旧问题**：Qwen3-Omni 的音频 tower 总是 eager 执行。ASR clips 短（约 100–3000 tokens），但 32 层小 varlen-attention 和 MLP kernel 形成 launch-bound，负载下出现很长的 encoder tail 和 P95/P99 上升。  
- **核心技术机制**：将 `Qwen3OmniMoeAudioEncoder.forward` 拆为三个方法：`embed_audio_features`（conv frontend + positional embedding）保持 eager；`prepare_encoder_metadata`（窗口 `cu_seqlens`/`max_seqlen`）；`forward_transformer`（固定形状张量，进入 CUDA graph）。CUDA graph 覆盖 transformer layers 和 output MLP；budget 从 104 tokens 到 `min(max_num_batched_tokens, max_model_len)`，由已有 `encoder_cudagraph_max_token_budget`（默认 5120）封顶。padding windows 重复最后一个 offset 使其 attend 到空；仅 FLASH_ATTN/TRITON_ATTN 启用。  
- **与已有路线的差别**：现有 `cudagraph_mm_encoder` 只覆盖视觉 tower，此 PR 扩展到音频，复用同一个 `SupportsEncoderCudaGraph`/`EncoderCudaGraphManager`，无新配置项。  
- **可信程度**：PR body 自述，有实验数据但未看到合并状态或独立验证。1×B200、Qwen3-Omni 30B-A3B ASR fine-tune：encoder p95 由 7.07ms（eager FA）降到 2.20ms，p99 由 9.87ms 降到 2.65ms；E2E P95 在 80 req/s 下从 198.5ms 降到 171.8ms（第二次跑 163.7ms）；capture 34 graphs，1.73s，322MiB。需要查证与 FlashInfer/ROCm 的边界及合并后回归。  
- **对 VLA/系统的启示**：VLA 常含语音指令/环境音频等短序列编码器，launch-bound 会显著抬高感知端延迟。将 encoder graph 与 decoder graph 分离、用 budget 桶管理可变长度是直接可复用的办法。异步控制中，音频/视觉感知的 P99 延迟会直接进入 action 输出周期，CUDA graph 消除长尾应作为具身部署的默认优化。

---

### 5. SGLang：FlashInfer MoE 与 MegaMoE 的 Prefill CUDA Graphs  
- **原始材料**：[Feat] [NVIDIA] cuda-graph: Prefill CUDA graphs for FlashInfer CuTe DSL MoE and MegaMoE；2026-11-20；PR body；https://github.com/sgl-project/sglang/pull/50684  
- **旧问题**：FlashInfer CuTe DSL MoE 与 MegaMoE 的 prefill CUDA graph 集成此前只在禁用图模式下验证，e2e 测试被迫 eager；`--enable-memory-saver` 与 breakable prefill graphs 冲突；`SGLANG_FLASHINFER_AUTOTUNE_EXTEND=1` 对 speculative targets 静默失效；EXTEND dummy 序列尺寸可能超过 per-rank ceiling 导致 FlashInfer A2A dispatcher assert。  
- **核心技术机制**：MegaMoE 加入 breakable CUDA graph 的 a2a allowlist，DP prefill batch 在所有 rank 上 pad 到共享 MAX_LEN bucket，使每个 rank 捕获到的 MegaMoE 调用用相同 workspace profile；`BreakableCUDAGraphCapture` 增加 `segment_capture` 上下文工厂，在 memory-saver 模式下用 `torch_memory_saver` 的 pauseable `cuda_graph` 分段捕获；speculative target 的 dummy run 保留 `ForwardMode.EXTEND` 而非强制 `TARGET_VERIFY`；EXTEND dummy 改为用能均分 N 的 seqs × tokens 组合，保证恰好到达 per-rank ceiling；Nemotron-H 在 SM100 系列加入支持（opt-in）。  
- **与已有路线的差别**：不是新 attention 算法，而是把 breakable CUDA graphs、memory saver、FlashInfer MoE 与投机解码 autotune 的边界条件打通。  
- **可信程度**：PR body 自述，主要描述修复和测试范围，未给性能数字；未确认合并或 CI 通过。需要查证 PR 最终讨论与合并状态。  
- **对 VLA/系统的启示**：VLA 的 prefill 常包含多模态上下文、长程规划，极易回退 eager。可打破图 + 内存暂停/恢复的组合适合长上下文重载、多任务切换和投机解码；分段捕获避免 memory saver 把图池分配抢走。异步控制中，如果 VLA 模型包含 MoE 层，需验证图捕获在数据并行下是否一致，否则 prefill/decode 交替会造成隐性 eager 回退和延迟尖峰。

---

### 6. HF Blog：180B MoE 在 32GB 内存上流式专家  
- **原始材料**：180B Parameters, 32GB of RAM: Pushing MoE Inference to the Limit with Transformers；2026-11-18；开发者博客（正文可见）；https://huggingface.co/blog/moe-expert-streaming  
- **旧问题**：在统一内存受限（M5 32GB）的 Mac 上跑 121GB 专家的 MoE 模型，llama.cpp/vLLM/Transformers 的 offload 方案不是太慢，就是无法容纳 n-gram 表等模型特定组件。  
- **核心技术机制**：把专家放磁盘，设备上建立 slot pool——预分配一个共享 device tensor，所有层共用，并维护每层 expert id 到 slot 的表；把 router 的 expert id 重映射到 slot，使 `grouped_mm` 直接在该 slot pool 上运行，无需自定义 expert matmul。miss 由 8 个 I/O 线程连续读，提前运行下两层 router 做专家预取；专家量化到 3 bits，dense 层 8 bits，n-gram 表按行从磁盘读；MPS 上通过提前 commit GPU 工作减少空转；为 Gated DeltaNet/hyper-connections 写 Metal kernel。  
- **与已有路线的差别**：相比 vLLM 的 CPU offload 只流式传输 routed experts，并通过 slot pool 保持 `grouped_mm` 兼容；相比 Strata，差距约 6%（短 decode 13.9 vs 14.8 tok/s，prefill 略快）。  
- **可信程度**：开发者博客自述，提供个人实验数据和 Space，但无独立验证；声称通用实现已进入 `huggingface/transformers#50717`，但未确认合并。数字为作者在其 M5 上自测，不能视为普遍性能。  
- **对 VLA/系统的启示**：边缘/本地运行大型 MoE VLA 时，专家热缓存 + 路由预取可大幅降低显存需求。异步控制中，专家 miss 会带来 SSD 延迟，需要根据 router 置信度或提前预算保证控制频率。slot pool 重映射体现“缓存友好的专家布局”，对异构内存 GPU 推理系统的 MoE 层设计有参考价值。

---

### 跨领域弱信号与趋势假设  
**弱信号**：TensorRT-LLM v1.3.0（https://github.com/NVIDIA/TensorRT-LLM/releases/tag/v1.3.0）作为 release notes（metadata only）同时引入 Rubin preview、DeepSeek-V4/Kimi K3、MXFP8、NVFP4 KV cache compression、Router Replay（返回 per-token routing 给 RL 训练）等，说明 MoE 路由感知与量化/流式正在同时向训练数据层和消费级硬件下沉；vLLM ROCm PR 61214 则显示 MI300X 上 MXFP8 MoE 专家权重减半。这不是孤立优化，而是“专家驻留位置由路由决定”的基础设施转向。

**趋势假设 1**：未来 6–12 个月，VLA 安全评估会普遍增加“中间状态接管 + 物理事件”维度，初始状态拒绝或未完成不再算安全。SAFI 的 fallback target 思路可能进入 fine-tuning 流程。  
*置信度*：中高。  
*可反证实验*：在真实机器人上复现 SAFI，检查 hold 是否导致滑动或 retained 技能退化；若出现新类型的物理事件或 retained-task 成功率显著下降，则假设需要修正。

**趋势假设 2**：世界模型的“动作敏感性”会成为具身规划系统的默认训练辅助目标，推理系统需要支持多候选动作的并行 rollout 与值估计。  
*置信度*：中。  
*可反证实验*：在闭环 VLA 规划中比较 AFFECT 与 baseline 世界模型，测量 real-to-sim 政策成功率相关性和端到端任务成功；若相关性提升不转化为实际任务收益，或带来不可接受的推理延迟，则假设弱化。

**趋势假设 3**：多模态编码器和 MoE 的 CUDA graph/流式缓存会从 LLM serving 扩展到 VLA 部署，典型栈将分离感知 encoder graph 与行动 decoder/扩散 rollout，用 budget bucket 和专家预取管理尾部延迟与显存。  
*置信度*：中。  
*可反证实验*：在真实机器人上测量音频/视觉 encoder CUDA graph 对动作输出 P99 的影响，以及 MoE 专家 miss 对控制频率的影响；若 encoder graph 未带来端到端收益或专家 miss 频率不可控，则趋势需要打折扣。

---

### 本周值得精读的 2 篇  
1. **SAFI**：https://huggingface.co/papers/2611.26239  
   理由：它把 VLA 安全从“初始状态拒绝”拉到“执行中途接管”，直接改变安全评测和 fallback 系统设计；方法简单（动作块监督 + 联合适应），但验证了中间状态评估的必要性。  
2. **AFFECT**：https://huggingface.co/papers/2611.25980  
   理由：世界模型的“动力学忠实度”是 VLA 离线评估与 model-based planning 的基石；AFFECT 给出的 action perturbation 匹配思路可能成为世界模型训练的常规组件，值得仔细核对其实验与可扩展性。

---
**本次采集**：共采集 419 条，去重后 419 条；候选池 120 条，本次精选 9 条。源异常 1 处（见仓库 Actions 日志）。

selected.summary: ## Motivation The FlashInfer CuTe DSL MoE (`flashinfer_cutedsl`, NVFP4 W4A4 and W4A16) and FlashInfer MegaMoE W4A16 (`flashinfer_megamoe`) integrations (#28354, #35120, #43789, #44036) were validated with prefill CUDA graphs disabled: their e2e tests passed `--cuda-graph-backend-prefill disabled`, and the CuTe DSL tests never ran the full-model EXTEND autotune pass. This PR runs those tests with breakable prefill CUDA graphs (BCG; the default backend, passed explicitly for the Nemotron-H classes), runs the CuTe DSL GSM8K tests with `SGLANG_FLASHINFER_AUTOTUNE_EXTEND=1`, and fixes the gaps that blocked, broke, or silently disabled either one. ## Modifications - **MegaMoE prefill graphs:** add `flashinfer_megamoe` to the BCG a2a allowlist in `disable_breakable_cudagraph_if_incompatible`. Before, any server using it fell back to eager prefill ("unvalidated a2a backend"). MegaMoE keeps the generic DP contract: a DP prefill graph batch is padded to one shared MAX_LEN bucket on every rank (an idle rank runs a dummy extend of that bucket), so every rank's captured MegaMoE call uses the same workspace profile; the per-rank SUM_LEN replay in `prefill_graph_tolerates_sum_len` stays DeepGEMM-`megamoe`-only. - **BCG under the memory saver:** `BreakableCudaGraphBackend` raised `NotImplementedError` with `--enable-memory-saver` + `SGLANG_MEMORY_SAVER_CUDA_GRAPH=1`, which is why the RL reload test disabled prefill graphs. `BreakableCUDAGraphCapture` now takes an optional `segment_capture` context factory that captures each segment; in memory-saver mode it is `torch_memory_saver`'s pauseable `cuda_graph(tag="cuda_graph", enable_cpu_backup=True)`, the same capture the full backend uses for each graph. `release_memory_occupation`/`resume_memory_occupation` with the `cuda_graph` tag then free and restore breakable graph memory, including capture-time state that replays read. Default capture (no memory saver) is unchanged. XPU and NPU still reject the combination at startup: the pauseable capture wraps `torch.cuda.graph` only (XPU's is a no-op), and the NPU breakable prefill backend added in #49481 subclasses this backend. - Why per segment: `torch_memory_saver.region()` also redirects the thread's allocations to its own pool, which would take capture allocations away from the shared graph pool between segments; `cuda_graph()` only marks the graph pool's allocations as pauseable. - **EXTEND autotune for speculative targets:** `maybe_flashinfer_autotune_extend` returned early for every speculative target, so `SGLANG_FLASHINFER_AUTOTUNE_EXTEND=1` silently did nothing under EAGLE/MTP (#36219 left speculative configs as a follow-up). A target prefills with plain EXTEND forwards, so `_dummy_run` now keeps an explicit `ForwardMode.EXTEND` override for a target instead of forcing TARGET_VERIFY, reusing the path PD prefill targets already take. Draft workers and the decode-shaped dummy are unchanged. - **EXTEND dummy sizing:** when the attention backend caps dummy sequences by the request pool (`extend_dummy_seqs_capped_by_req_pool`), the dummy rounded up to `ceil(N/pool)` tokens per sequence, which can exceed the per-rank ceiling `N` that serving never exceeds. With Nemotron-H's 12-slot pool, N=4096 became 12 x 342 = 4104 tokens and the FlashInfer one-sided A2A dispatcher (sized for 4096 per rank) asserted at startup. The dummy now uses the most sequences, up to the pool size, that split `N` evenly (here 8 x 512), so it reaches exactly the ceiling. - **Nemotron-H prefill graphs on SM100-family (opt-in):** `NemotronHModel.supports_hybrid_prefill_graph` was `is_sm120()`, so on B200/B300 the target logged "Disable prefill CUDA graph because some layers do not apply Standard GQA" and both Nemotron CuTe DSL tests prefilled eagerly. selected.summary: ## Overview DiffusionGemma batches mix causal requests (prompt and commit) with bidirectional requests (denoise). On SM100-family GPUs, vLLM had no fast backend for these batches: - FlashInfer rejected the model. - The default backend, FA4, fails at startup because its per-request causal mask is SM90-only. So B200 users had to pass `--attention-backend TRITON_ATTN`. This PR runs the mixed batches on FlashInfer TRTLLM-Gen and makes that the default for text-only serving (`--language-model-only`) on SM100-family GPUs. It needs https://github.com/flashinfer-ai/flashinfer/pull/4905 (VariableWindow FMHA), which is in FlashInfer 0.7.3 and later (vLLM pins 0.7.4). **Scope:** SM100 family, text-only serving. Hopper and multimodal serving keep their current backend choice. ## Claims - **Perf:** 1.10–1.45× (BF16 KV) and 1.15–1.54× (FP8 KV) output tokens/s per GPU over `TRITON_ATTN` with BF16 KV, on 1×B200 at concurrency 1–8. - **Accuracy:** GPQA-Diamond scores 68.69 (BF16 KV) and 69.67 (FP8 KV), against 69.95 for `TRITON_ATTN`. - **Default:** `vllm serve --language-model-only` now selects FlashInfer TRTLLM-Gen on SM100 with no attention flag. selected.summary: ## Overview Adds the `aiter_triton_mxfp8_mxfp8` MoE backend, so MXFP8 MoE models run on MI300X / MI325X (gfx942) with their expert weights kept in MXFP8. Today these models fall back to `EMULATION` on gfx942, which unpacks every expert weight to BF16. vLLM picks it automatically on gfx942. `--moe-backend aiter_triton_mxfp8_mxfp8` pins it. Needs ROCm/aiter#6219, which ships in the current nightly (aiter `0.1.29`). ## Results On `tencent/Hy4-preview-FP8`, TP8, MI325X, compared with the current nightly: - Expert weights take about half the memory: 109 GiB per GPU instead of 196 GiB. This is what lets Hy4 fit on 192 GB MI300X. - 4x more KV cache (2.69M tokens instead of 688K). - 13 to 23% more output throughput at 8K, 32K and 128K input. - Same GSM8K accuracy (96.8% on both). ### Hy4-preview-FP8, TP8 | | Nightly (`EMULATION`) | This PR | |---|---|---| | Model memory per GPU | 195.8 GiB | **109.1 GiB** | | KV cache | 688K tokens | **2.69M tokens** | | GSM8K, 5-shot, 1319 questions | 96.82% | 96.82% | | Input / output / concurrency | Output tok/s | TTFT | TPOT | |---|---|---|---| | 8K / 1K / 16 | 308.9 → **369.0** (+19%) | 5.3 → 5.4 s | 46.7 → **38.1 ms** | | 32K / 1K / 16 | 174.4 → **197.7** (+13%) | 14.3 → 14.5 s | 77.7 → **66.7 ms** | | 128K / 1K / 8 | 46.1 → **56.5** (+23%) | 82.6 → **42.0 s** | **84.5** → 100.4 ms | At 128K the time per token goes up while total throughput still goes up. My guess is that faster prefill lets more requests decode at the same time, but I have not confirmed it. ### MiniMax-M3.1-Flash, TP4 This checkpoint ships NVFP4 experts, which ROCm can't run directly, so vLLM requantizes them at load with `--quantization-config.moe`. | MoE setting | GSM8K | 8K / 1K / 16 | 32K / 1K / 16 | 128K / 1K / 8 | |---|---|---|---|---| | `mxfp8`, nightly (`EMULATION`) | did not finish (1 h 27 min for 88%) | 24.5 tok/s | 23.0 tok/s* | 10.7 tok/s* | | `mxfp8`, this PR | 95.91% | 453.8 tok/s | 266.1 tok/s | 85.6 tok/s | | `fp8_per_channel`, nightly (AITER FP8) | 95.83% | 536.2 tok/s | 308.3 tok/s | 100.1 tok/s | \* single batch only; the full run was too slow. With `mxfp8` this PR is 8 to 18x faster than today. `fp8_per_channel` is still about 15% faster on MiniMax, so it stays the better choice there. selected.title: 180B Parameters, 32GB of RAM: Pushing MoE Inference to the Limit with Transformers
selected.text: Back to Articles 180B Parameters, 32GB of RAM: Pushing MoE Inference to the Limit with Transformers Published November 18, 2026 Update on GitHub Upvote 29 +23 Tarek Ziadé tarekziade Follow Streaming MoE experts directly from SSD gets within 6% of Strata on token generation. I've been trying to rely less on online models and run bigger ones locally. At home I have a PC with two RTX 4090s (let's call it Orthrus - the two-headed hound of Greek mythology), and for work I have a MacBook M5 with 32G of unified memory. Orthrus runs on Windows 11, because my kids play games all the time. I had a dual boot with Ubuntu, but their games ended up taking most of the two terabytes of disk. I am also a huge fan of RMD (rooms moving development): one hour in the kitchen sipping my coffee, two hours at my office desk, then the sofa. A fixed desktop tower is not for me. My first experiment was to run Qwen 3.8 27B with llama.app on Orthrus and use it from my laptop through pi . That model does the coding tasks, an online model like Opus does the orchestration, and the second RTX runs a FIM model for auto-completion in Neovim. When I talked about this on social networks, I got very strong feedback: use Strata with Qwen3.8-Flash-Next . What is Strata? Strata is an inference engine for MoE models like Qwen. Only the hot experts stay in VRAM, the rest goes to RAM, or even to disk. Experts are 90%+ of a MoE model's weights, so a 180B model like this one can run on a GPU with much less memory. Like my RTX 4090! It works on a laptop too, and I stumbled on this blog post doing exactly that: Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on a 32 GB Mac M4, faster than llama.cpp , at 13.5 tok/s. That's too slow for how I use coding agents, but it's an interesting itch to scratch. A whole range of MoE models don't fit in a MacBook's unified memory and could run at a decent speed. How do other engines offload? Before committing to Strata, I looked at what llama.cpp, vLLM and Transformers do when a MoE model doesn't fit. Three questions matter: where do the experts live, where does the expert matmul run, and what moves on each token? llama.cpp maps the GGUF file with mmap and can keep the experts on the CPU ( --cpu-moe , --n-cpu-moe N , -ot "exps=CPU" , or --fit on to pick for you). Those experts are also computed on the CPU, so only the activations cross PCIe, never the weights. Great when the experts fit in RAM. When they don't, the page cache thrashes. A GPU expert cache ( --moe-cache-mib ) just landed, but it fragments the graph (2 splits per token become 50) and loses ~10% even when everything fits. vLLM 's --cpu-offload-gb N puts N GB of weights in pinned RAM, and kernels read them in place over PCIe. For a MoE layer, that's only the routed experts, but nothing is cached: a hot expert crosses PCIe again on every token, and there's no disk tier. By default the offloaded weights include dense layers, read on every token; --cpu-offload-params experts keeps it to the experts. That fits vLLM's big batches, which touch almost every expert anyway, less so one user on one GPU. Transformers offloads through Accelerate ( device_map="auto" , offload_folder ), one module at a time: hooks copy its weights to the GPU before forward . For a MoE, that module is a layer's whole expert bank, so every token copies every expert of every offloaded layer to use 8 or 10 of them. No cache, no notion of routing. And on a Mac, CPU and GPU share the same memory, so "offload to CPU" frees nothing. I ran all of them on Qwen3.6-35B-A3B on one A10G (24 GB), with plenty of RAM, and Harry Mellor reran vLLM with better flags: Engine Decode (tok/s) Strata, Q8_0 82 - 88 llama.cpp, Q8_0, --fit on 63 - 64 llama.cpp, BF16, --fit on 35 - 36 vLLM, FP8, --cpu-offload-gb 16 --cpu-offload-params experts 20.1 vLLM, FP8, same flags, --enforce-eager 14.7 vLLM, FP8, --cpu-offload-gb 16 9.7 vLLM, BF16, --cpu-offload-gb 50 --cpu-offload-params experts 7.3 vLLM, BF16, --cpu-offload-gb 50 3.3 Transformers + Accelerate 0.16 Offloading only the experts doubles vLLM's speed, and FP8 helps on top (half the bytes per expert, more of the model on the GPU). vLLM's other offload backend, which copies groups of layers ahead of time, ran under 1 tok/s. If the experts fit in RAM, llama.cpp is hard to beat. If they don't, you have to stream only what the router picks, through a bounded cache, fast enough that the SSD is the bottleneck and not Python, ideally reusing the model's fast expert kernels. That's Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on a 32 GB Mac, and Transformers couldn't do it out of the box. Making Qwen3.8-Flash-Next work on my 32 GB Mac with Transformers Strata was already too slow for me on the laptop, and Transformers was not going to beat it anytime soon. But the Accelerate path was so far off that I wanted to try fixing offloading in Transformers itself, with the big model on my laptop as the target, knowing it would probably stay too slow for how I work. All of the code was built with AI: the Transformers PR, the model-specific package and the Metal kernels. My part was choosing what to try, reading the profiles, and deciding what to keep. Everything is in a Space: tarekziade/moe-expert-streaming . Start small I started with OLMoE-1B-7B , which fits in memory, so I could compare every token with vanilla Transformers. First version: experts on disk, an LRU cache on the device, and a Python loop running one expert at a time. With every expert already cached, it did 10.1 tok/s. Vanilla did ~32. The I/O was fine, my loop was not: vanilla uses grouped_mm , which runs all the experts of a layer in one kernel. The fix, and the key idea of this project, was to turn the cache into a slot pool : one preallocated device tensor shared by all layers, plus a per-layer table from expert id to slot. Remap the router's expert ids to slots and the pool looks like a regular expert bank, so grouped_mm runs on it as is. No custom expert matmul needed. That got it to 34.6 tok/s, against 38.1 for vanilla. experts_offload I then turned the standalone loader into an option of from_pretrained , in huggingface/transformers#50717 . To try it, install Transformers from that PR: pip install "git+https://github.com/huggingface/transformers.git@refs/pull/50717/head" Then, moving from OLMoE to the real target, Qwen3.8-Flash-Next: path = snapshot_download( "tarekziade/Qwen3.8-Flash-Next-expert-streaming" ) model = AutoModelForCausalLM.from_pretrained( f" {path} /dense" , dtype=torch.bfloat16, device_map={ "" : "mps" , "experts.*" : "disk" }, quantization_config=MetalConfig(bits= 8 ), experts_offload={ "cache_bytes" : 12 << 30 , "quantized_experts" : f" {path} /experts-q3" , }, ) That repo holds the output of the project's conversion script : the dense weights, the experts quantized to 3 bits, and the n-gram table. Experts mapped to "disk" go through the streaming path instead of Accelerate's offload: the loader skips their tensors and MoE layers switch to an offloaded implementation. Misses are read by 8 I/O threads, one contiguous read per expert. The next two layers' routers run early on the current hidden states to guess which experts to prefetch. Experts can be quantized offline so reads are smaller. It works for MoE models with the standard experts layout. The API is still being discussed with the Transformers maintainers. The device_map form came out of that, and quantized experts will probably go through the per-layer quantization plan of #50245 rather than their own option. Running 121 GB of experts on a 32 GB Mac Qwen3.8-Flash-Next has 48 layers of 512 experts (10 active), 121 GB in FP8. Streaming them isn't enough: there's also a 51 GB n-gram embedding table that needs its own disk path. So: experts quantized to 3 bits: 49 GB on disk, 12 GiB cached on the device dense layers in 8 bits (~5.4 GB, +0.2% perplexity vs BF16) the n-gram table stays on disk, rows read when needed The conversion takes ~5 hours. After loading, it uses ~18 GiB, and a 6K prompt peaks at 25.4 GiB. That's about the limit: I have to close the browser, or macOS starts swapping. The model-specific bits (the n-gram table, Metal kernels) live in a small package, moe-expert-streaming , on top of the PR. The first version ran at about 10 tok/s. Then I installed Strata on the same M5, with the same prompts: Transformers Strata Gap Decode, 200 tokens 10.0 tok/s 14.8 1.5x Prefill, 4K prompt 68 tok/s 220 3.2x Decode after a 6K document 7.3 tok/s 13.7 1.9x Strata 0.1.60 used IQ3_XXS experts. Both ran greedy, with thinking, MTP and speculative drafts off, and 1,024-token prefill chunks. The full setup and raw results are on the Space's details page . I also tried vllm-metal , vLLM on Apple GPUs through MLX, which recently got expert offloading. It streams the routed experts from an MLX checkpoint through a bounded cache, like this project. But it can't run Qwen3.8-Flash-Next on 32 GB, for the n-gram reason above: only the experts are streamed, and the n-gram tables stay in memory. That's 32 GB in the MLX checkpoints on the Hub, before the ~5 GB of dense layers and any expert cache. Closing the gap Most of the time wasn't spent on experts. Here's what helped: Committing GPU work early. PyTorch on MPS holds small kernels until the next sync, so the GPU idled while Python worked. Forcing a commit after each block gave +10%. This should really be fixed in PyTorch. Metal kernels for the parts without a fast path on macOS: Gated DeltaNet and the hyper-connections. Strata's own weights. I switched to Strata's GGUF weights , reducing dense weight traffic from 5.4 GB to 3.9 GB per token and individual expert size from 2.15 MB to 1.75 MB, with a separate cache pool for each expert size. Prefill , we went from 68 to ~228 tok/s using bigger chunks, and reading the next layer's experts while the current layer is being computed. Long documents : attention over the indexer's selected blocks only, and a KV cache that grows in place instead of being copied at every token. Misses : Strata doesn't hide them, it waits like I do, and no cache policy beat LRU by much. What helped was reading just one guessed expert per layer, while the SSD would otherwise be idle. Here's one MoE layer for one token, as it runs now: These are the final results after these optimizations on the same M5 with the same prompts: Transformers Strata Gap Decode, 200 tokens 13.9 tok/s 14.8 1.06x Prefill, 4K prompt 228 tok/s 220 1.0x Decode after a 6K document 12.4 tok/s 13.7 1.1x That's about 6% behind Strata on short decode, with slightly faster prefill, all through Transformers. Most of what's left is host round trips, ~10 ms per token. Waking up after a sync is only ~1 ms of that. The rest is the GPU running dry while Python queues the next layer. Strata queues the whole token's work up front, and the GPU waits on a Metal shared event at each layer while the host reads experts. PyTorch doesn't expose that. I tried to fake it with a kernel spinning on a flag the CPU writes, and the GPU took anywhere from a second to never to see the write. The real fix would be a native op on PyTorch's MPS stream, with a risk of hangs, so I haven't built it. Conclusion It runs at ~14 tok/s, close to Strata, and it's still too slow for how I use coding agents. Orthrus keeps doing the real work. Transformers didn't beat Strata, and closing the last ~6% would take deeper changes in the stack, starting with control over that per-layer sync, which PyTorch doesn't give you today. The interesting part is how it got that close: streaming only the routed experts, a bounded cache that grouped_mm runs on as is, and a few targeted Metal kernels. There's no C++ extension in the project: just Python, Metal kernels compiled at runtime with torch.mps.compile_shader , and prebuilt kernels from the Hub . All the Metal kernels written for this experiment are now published on the Hub , and the project loads them from there. Beating Strata was never the only goal, though. Building this was a great way to learn how MoEs and LLMs work from a systems perspective: how sparse the routing really is, how much an expert cache buys you, where memory bandwidth goes per token, and how much time the host and the GPU spend waiting on each other. Transformers makes all of that easy to poke at, one module at a time. The generic expert streaming implementation is in huggingface/transformers#50717 , and the benchmarks are in the Space . Feedback on the approach and the API is welcome. Thanks to Pedro, Lysandre and Arthur for their excellent feedback, and to Harry for helping test vLLM. Finally, thanks to Niko Veit for Strata . Strata set the bar for what's possible with expert streaming on consumer hardware, and having those numbers to chase is what pushed this work as far as it went. selected.title: Teaching Vision-Language-Action Models to Stop Safely
selected.summary: Vision-language-action (VLA) models enable robots to perform diverse tasks from visual observations and language instructions. While prior work has explored task suppression and refusal, stopping prohibited behavior once execution is underway and controlling the resulting physical response remain challenging. Our evaluation reveals that policies which suppress a task from its initial state can still complete it when taking over partway through execution. Even when the task remains unfinished, the robot may drop a held object, making non-completion an incomplete measure of safety. To address these challenges, we introduce State-Aware Fallback Imitation (SAFI) for tasks where holding provides an appropriate alternative response. SAFI comprises two stages, (1) fallback target construction, which assigns stationary arm commands and consistent gripper targets throughout prohibited-task demonstrations, and (2) joint policy adaptation, which learns these targets alongside the original actions of retained tasks. This supervision teaches an explicit alternative response at intermediate execution states while maintaining the robot's other skills. Extensive experiments with OpenVLA-OFT across LIBERO and BadLIBERO tasks evaluate prohibited completion, physical incidents, and retained-task performance. On the evaluated LIBERO tasks, SAFI reduces aggregate target success after takeover to 1.3\%, with no recorded physical incidents or action saturation, while preserving high retained-task success.
selected.text: Teaching Vision-Language-Action Models to Stop Safely Zheyuan Liu Affiliation: University of Notre Dame Email: zliu29@nd.edu Chuhan Wang Affiliation: University of Notre Dame Jinduo Guo Affiliation: University of Notre Dame Yue Huang Affiliation: University of Notre Dame Xiangchi Yuan Affiliation: Georgia Tech Ningshan Ma Affiliation: MIT Meng Jiang Affiliation: University of Notre Dame Abstract Vision-language-action (VLA) models enable robots to perform diverse tasks from visual observations and language instructions. While prior work has explored task suppression and refusal, stopping prohibited behavior once execution is underway and controlling the resulting physical response remain challenging. Our evaluation reveals that policies which suppress a task from its initial state can still complete it when taking over partway through execution. Even when the task remains unfinished, the robot may drop a held object, making non-completion an incomplete measure of safety. To address these challenges, we introduce State-Aware Fallback Imitation (SAFI) for tasks where holding provides an appropriate alternative response. SAFI comprises two stages, (1) fallback target construction, which assigns stationary arm commands and consistent gripper targets throughout prohibited-task demonstrations, and (2) joint policy adaptation, which learns these targets alongside the original actions of retained tasks. This supervision teaches an explicit alternative response at intermediate execution states while maintaining the robot’s other skills. Extensive experiments with OpenVLA-OFT across LIBERO and BadLIBERO tasks evaluate prohibited completion, physical incidents, and retained-task performance. On the evaluated LIBERO tasks, SAFI reduces aggregate target success after takeover to 1.3%, with no recorded physical incidents or action saturation, while preserving high retained-task success. 1 1 1 Code is available at franciscoliu/SAFI . 1 Introduction Figure 1: Two possible responses after takeover from the same holding state. Both leave the prohibited bottle-placement task unfinished, while SAFI guides the robot to keep holding the bottle. Vision-language-action (VLA) models connect visual observations and language instructions to robot control ( Zitkovich et al., 2023 ; Kim et al., 2025b ; Qu et al., 2025 ) , building on robot demonstration learning ( Brohan et al., 2023 ) and multimodal task grounding ( Driess et al., 2023 ; Jiang et al., 2023 ) . Generalist policies extend these capabilities across robot platforms and unfamiliar environments ( Ghosh et al., 2024 ; Black et al., 2025b ; Black et al., 2025a ) , while action-sequence prediction and efficient fine-tuning improve manipulation performance ( Zhao et al., 2023 ; Chi et al., 2023 ; Kim et al., 2025a ; Cui et al., 2026a ) . As these policies acquire more skills, deployment also requires control over which learned behaviors remain appropriate to execute. This requirement becomes concrete when context makes an otherwise feasible action hazardous. Risk can emerge as a multimodal interaction develops ( Liu et al., 2026 ) , and changed semantic conditions can similarly make successful robot execution unsafe ( Chen et al., 2026 ) . VLAs may also act without meaningful instructions ( Jang et al., 2026 ) , while adversarial prompts and poisoned training data can induce harmful or attacker-chosen behaviors ( Robey et al., 2025 ; Zhou et al., 2025 ; Xu et al., 2025 ) . Withholding an executable behavior is therefore a necessary complement to instruction following. Planning methods support this control through robot affordances ( Ichter et al., 2023 ) , uncertainty-based requests for help ( Ren et al., 2023 ) , and contextual safety specifications ( Ravichandran et al., 2026 ) . At the policy level, constrained learning ( Zhang et al., 2025 ) and refusal demonstrations ( Chen et al., 2026 ) teach safer responses. Selective unlearning offers another route by reducing unwanted behavior while preserving useful capabilities in language models ( Yao et al., 2024 ; Liu et al., 2024 ) and VLAs ( Ranjan and Polyzou, 2026 ; Wang et al., 2026 ) . Since earlier actions determine later observations in sequential control ( Ross et al., 2011 ) , evaluation from initial states can leave intermediate states untested when an edited policy stops before reaching them. We examine these states by transferring control from the original policy during execution. This reveals a failure to stop ongoing tasks , as several policies that suppress completion from initial states still complete the prohibited task after takeover. Even when it remains unfinished, unsafe alternative responses arise, including dropping a held bottle (Figure 1 ). Dropping and holding both prevent placement but have different physical consequences. These observations, developed in Section 2 , motivate the following research question. How can VLAs stop ongoing prohibited tasks while maintaining an appropriate physical response? Addressing this requires models to suppress prohibited behavior across execution states and produce an alternative response suited to the robot’s current state. To meet these requirements, we propose State-Aware Fallback Imitation (SAFI) for tasks where holding provides an appropriate alternative. Its two-stage design combines Fallback Target Construction , which assigns holding targets throughout prohibited-task demonstrations, with Joint Policy Adaptation , which learns these targets alongside the original actions of retained tasks. By learning an explicit fallback across execution states, SAFI enables the robot to stop prohibited tasks with a holding response while preserving its other skills. Our main contributions are as follows. 1. We identify failures to stop ongoing tasks and unsafe alternative responses in VLAs through an intermediate-state takeover evaluation that jointly examines prohibited execution and physical events. 2. We propose SAFI, a two-stage framework that constructs fallback targets from prohibited-task demonstrations and jointly optimizes fallback and retained-task imitation to suppress prohibited behavior and learn an appropriate alternative response while preserving permitted skills. 3. We evaluate SAFI across multiple LIBERO task suites and a BadLIBERO backdoor setting. On the evaluated LIBERO tasks, SAFI achieves low prohibited-task completion rates after takeover with no recorded drops or falls, while preserving performance on retained tasks. 2 Motivations Failure to Stop Ongoing Tasks. Our first motivation is inspired by findings that safety-aligned language models can continue harmful responses when given their opening text, despite normally refusing such requests ( Qi et al., 2025 ) . This raises a related question for VLAs about whether suppressing a prohibited task also prevents its continuation once execution is underway. To examine this, we let the original policy begin a task and then transfer control to a policy trained to suppress it. As shown in Figure 2 (a), some evaluated policies prevent prohibited stove activation from the initial state, yet activate the stove in nearly all episodes after early takeover and all episodes after mid-task takeover. These results show that suppression from initial states does not reliably prevent continuation of the same prohibited task once execution is underway. Unsafe Alternative Responses. A second challenge is about what a robot does when a forbidden task remains unfinished. Prior work distinguishes execution failure from deliberate refusal, showing why low task success alone is an incomplete safety signal ( Chen et al., 2026 ) . Similarly, for a robot already holding an object, this distinction also involves the consequences of its alternative actions. In the example shown in Figure 2 (b), some evaluated policies leave the prohibited task unfinished but drop the held bottle. Both dropping the bottle and keeping it held satisfy the non-completion criterion, although their physical consequences differ. These findings reveal two challenges in enforcing behavioral prohibitions in VLAs: (1) suppression observed from initial states may fail after takeover , and (2) preventing task completion does not ensure an acceptable physical response . Addressing both challenges calls for an approach that suppresses the prohibited behavior across execution states and guides the robot toward an appropriate alternative response. Figure 2: Two gaps in task suppression on LIBERO-Goal. (a) Stove activation rates across initial and takeover states. (b) Cumulative bottle-drop rates over control steps after mid-task takeover. Some policies leave the task unfinished but drop the bottle. Events are recorded until rollout termination. 3 Method Figure 3: Overview of SAFI. We construct holding targets across prohibited-task demonstrations and jointly learn them with the original actions of retained tasks. Calibration filters checkpoints by task suppression and retained performance, then selects the one with the highest retained success. The response audit compares SAFI with baselines from initial and takeover states, examining task completion and physical outcomes. In this section, we present SAFI, a two-stage framework for adapting VLAs to behavioral prohibitions. The design addresses two challenges in enforcing these prohibitions: (1) failures to stop ongoing tasks and (2) unsafe alternative responses, as identified in Section 2 . Overview of SAFI. As shown in Figure 3 , Fallback Target Construction assigns holding responses across prohibited-task demonstrations. Joint Policy Adaptation then learns these targets alongside the original actions for retained tasks. 3.1 Fallback Target Construction The first stage defines an explicit response for the robot at each demonstrated state of a prohibited task. We use holding targets, building on explicit-response supervision in no-action fine-tuning and refusal training ( Jang et al., 2026 ; Chen et al., 2026 ) . Before training, we test a scripted hold from candidate takeover states and require it to prevent prohibited completion and satisfy the task-specific physical-event criteria. We apply SAFI to tasks that pass this applicability check. We use retained tasks to refer to the other permitted tasks whose performance we aim to preserve. Let 𝒟 p \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{p}} contain demonstrations of the behavior designated for suppression, to which we assign fallback targets, and let 𝒟 r \mathcal{D}_{\mathrm{r}} contain demonstrations whose original actions we preserve. On LIBERO, each edit targets one prohibited task and uses demonstrations of the other tasks in its suite for retained-task supervision. On BadLIBERO, the two sets contain poisoned and clean demonstrations, respectively, which can share task instructions. Each sample ( x , A ) (x,A) contains a policy input x x with camera observations, proprioception, and a task instruction, together with a normalized action chunk A ∈ ℝ H × d A\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times d} . Here, H H is the number of actions in a chunk and d d is the action dimension. Each action contains d − 1 d-1 robot-arm motion coordinates and one coordinate for opening or closing the gripper. To construct the fallback chunk A ¯ \bar{A} , we use a command that requests no change in the robot gripper’s position or orientation. We encode this motion command as a vector h ∈ ℝ d − 1 h\in\mathbb{R}^{d-1} using the demonstration’s action normalization. We assign this vector to every action in the chunk and repeat the first demonstrated gripper command throughout the chunk. For action index k = 1 , … , H k=1,\ldots,H and coordinate index j j , the target is A ¯ k , j = { h j , 1 ≤ j < d , A 1 , d , j = d . \bar{A}_{k,j}=\begin{cases}h_{j},&1\leq j<d,\\ A_{1,d},&j=d\end{cases}. (1) We apply Equation 1 throughout the prohibited-task demonstrations, pairing each input with its fallback chunk while preserving the observations and task instruction. These pairs provide supervision at intermediate as well as initial demonstration states, directly addressing the takeover setting in Section 2 . The action normalization and gripper-label details are provided in Appendix B.1 . 3.2 Joint Policy Adaptation The second stage teaches the policy to produce the constructed fallback targets while preserving its demonstrated actions on retained tasks. Yet despite producing increasingly realistic videos, current world models often fail to capture how small action changes affect future observations. This limits their use in tasks such as robotic policy evaluation and model-based planning, where nearly identical actions can lead to qualitatively different outcomes. Yet despite producing increasingly realistic videos, current world models often fail to capture how small action changes affect future observations. This limits their use in tasks such as robotic policy evaluation and model-based planning, where nearly identical actions can lead to qualitatively different outcomes. To address this, we propose AFFECT , an auxiliary training objective for learning the distribution of visual changes induced by action perturbations. Specifically, we inject temporally correlated noise into the actions of a policy trained on task-agnostic human teleoperation. We then train the world model so that its generated videos respond to this noise as the recorded videos do, without requiring repeated executions from the same initial state. Across OGBench simulation and real-world DROID and ALOHA-2 setups, AFFECT makes world-model rollouts more faithful to real outcomes. On DROID, the Pearson correlation between policy success rates in the world model and on the real robot rises from 0.47 to 0.79, alongside up to 23% lower FVD. These gains carry over to planning, where selecting actions with AFFECT -trained world models improves task success by up to 8.3 % 8.3\% . 1 Introduction Figure 1: Small action perturbations lead to distinct action effects. From the same initial state, actions drawn from a narrow distribution change the gripper’s approach only slightly, yet produce qualitatively different outcomes, where the cube is grasped, missed, or pushed away. A faithful world model must reproduce how these outcomes shift as the action is perturbed, rather than only rendering a plausible video for generic actions. World models ( Ha and Schmidhuber, 2018 ; Hafner et al., 2019 ; Hafner et al., 2025 ) predict future states conditioned on action sequences without execution in the environment. Recently, robotics world models (RWMs) ( Gao et al., 2026 ; Agarwal et al., 2026 ; Guo et al., 2026 ) realize this by building on video diffusion foundation models ( Wan et al., 2025 ; Ali et al., 2025 ; Kong et al., 2024 ) , generating photorealistic, temporally coherent videos conditioned on robot actions. This makes them a promising direction for diverse usage in evaluating policies ( Guo et al., 2026 ; Jeon et al., 2026 ) , planning manipulation trajectories ( Assran et al., 2025 ; Gao et al., 2026 ) , or generating training data ( Jang et al., 2025 ) . However, serving these roles requires robotics world models to faithfully reflect how small action changes alter future outcomes. For example, slight changes in reaching motion can determine whether a gripper grasps an object, misses it, or pushes it away (Figure 1 ). Yet existing models tend to produce visually plausible videos that ignore such differences ( Yang et al., 2026 ; Jiang et al., 2026 ) . Since such models predict similar outcomes for actions with different real consequences, they are unreliable as policy evaluators and mislead planners into selecting the wrong actions. Addressing this requires world models to acquire action sensitivity, and by extension, learn the relationship between action variations and resulting dynamics. We therefore treat action sensitivity as a distributional problem. Rather than simply reproducing recorded futures with high visual fidelity, we argue that an RWM should capture how the distribution of future observations shifts as actions vary under a given observation context. To learn such distributions, we introduce action variation directly into the training data. Specifically, we collect robot-environment interactions by running a policy trained on task-agnostic human teleoperation, in which an operator interacts freely with objects without a predefined task. Following Lynch et al. (2020) , we refer to such data as play data and to this policy as the play policy. During data collection, we inject temporally correlated noise into the action chunks produced by the play policy before rollout and log the injected perturbations. These rollouts expose how visual outcomes vary with action changes without requiring repeated executions from the same initial state or explicit outcome labels. Building on this data, we introduce AFFECT , an auxiliary training objective that teaches the world model the relationship between action changes and their visual consequences. AFFECT explicitly uses the noise injected into the training actions to supervise how generated visual outcomes should change with those action perturbations. In this way, the model is directly encouraged to respond to action variation in the same way as the real environment, rather than merely generating visually plausible futures. Since AFFECT operates on features from frozen encoders, it can be added to existing RWMs without architectural changes. We evaluate AFFECT on a simulated UR5e environment and two real-robot settings following the DROID ( Khazatsky et al., 2024 ) and ALOHA-2 ( Aldaco et al., 2024 ) configurations, and apply it to two distinct backbones, DreamDojo ( Gao et al., 2026 ) and Cosmos3 ( Agarwal et al., 2026 ) . To test whether the world model reflects action differences, we measure how well its predicted policy success rates correlate with real ones. On this measure, AFFECT improves every one of the six backbone–embodiment combinations, for instance raising the correlation of DreamDojo on DROID from 0.468 0.468 to 0.790 0.790 and that of Cosmos3 on ALOHA-2 from 0.298 0.298 to 0.694 0.694 . AFFECT also improves most visual metrics, including FVD reductions of up to 23 % 23\% on DROID and gains on every metric at both short and long horizons in simulation, suggesting that learning how actions shape outcomes also helps the model predict more realistic futures. Finally, this improved sensitivity translates into better model-based planning, where AFFECT raises task success rates by around 8 % 8\% on both UR5e pick-and-place and ALOHA-2 long-horizon tasks. 2 Preliminaries World model training. selected.title: Mind2Act World: A Diagnostic Benchmark for Embodied Mind, Physical Action, and Mind-Action Composition in Robotic Manipulation
selected.summary: Embodied intelligence aims to let robots perform complex physical tasks with human-like adaptability and reliability, which requires three complementary capabilities: history-based cognitive reasoning, precise and timely physical execution, and the composition of reasoning and execution through environmental feedback. Yet existing benchmarks either evaluate reasoning and execution within the same tasks or assess them separately without their composition, so they reveal little about whether a failure comes from reasoning, execution, or their composition. We introduce Mind2Act World, a diagnostic benchmark of 30 simulated manipulation tasks from five real-world application domains. Each task has three difficulty levels and two scene settings (Clean and Random), yielding 180 configurations. The tasks form three views: Mind tests decisions based on past observations, Act tests precise and timely execution, and Mind2Act combines both in closed-loop tasks where action outcomes guide later decisions. Comparing the three views shows whether a system lacks a capability or fails to compose capabilities it already has. A diagnosis harness further attributes the failed episodes of three representative systems to Mind, Act, or their composition and summarizes each system in a profile card. Our evaluation of multimodal agents, vision-language-action models (VLAs), and world-action models (WAMs) shows that competence in a single view does not carry over to Mind2Act tasks. Even the strongest agent succeeds in 52.7% of Mind and 39.0% of Act episodes but in only 12.0% of Mind2Act episodes. The strongest agent retains task state but struggles with sustained contact, whereas end-to-end policies execute practiced motions but retain little task state. These findings point to composing reasoning and execution through environmental feedback as the main open problem.

Studies of human sensorimotor control indicate that adaptive and reliable manipulation involves reasoning over task-relevant information, executing physical actions precisely, and adapting behavior through environmental feedback [ 1 , 2 , 3 ] . In the cooking task of Fig. , a robot must remember which ingredient to add next , coordinate both arms to add the ingredient , and switch the stove from heating to keep-warm mode based on temperature feedback . These requirements motivate three capabilities. Mind decides what to do from earlier observations. Act produces the required physical effect in time. Mind-Action Composition closes the loop, so that remembered information guides each action and each physical outcome updates the next decision. Recent embodied systems spanning multimodal agents [ 32 ] , vision-language-action models (VLAs) [ 19 , 20 ] , world-action models (WAMs) [ 23 , 26 ] , and hybrid architectures [ 27 , 28 ] have substantially advanced robotic manipulation. However, their capabilities in Mind , Act , and Mind-Action Composition remain poorly understood, which makes it difficult to identify capability bottlenecks and guide further development. Two limitations of existing embodied benchmarks [ 4 , 6 , 7 , 8 , 12 ] explain why. First, conventional benchmarks often assess cognitive reasoning and physical execution within the same tasks and report only whether a task succeeds [ 4 , 5 , 6 ] , so a failure cannot be traced to Mind or Act . Second, although recent benchmarks have introduced finer-grained diagnostics and separate assessments of reasoning and physical execution [ 8 , 11 , 12 , 13 ] , they rarely evaluate Mind-Action Composition , particularly whether physical outcomes can effectively inform subsequent decisions. Closing this gap requires tasks that stress one capability while keeping the others present but easy, a judgment of composition based on verified physical outcomes, and a comparison of systems with different action interfaces and inference speeds on equal terms. To this end, we introduce Mind2Act World , a diagnostic benchmark for Mind , Act , and Mind-Action Composition in robotic manipulation (Fig. ). Its 30 tasks come from five real-world application domains and are organized into three views of ten tasks each, covering 12 capability categories. Each view emphasizes one demand by design. Mind tasks keep physical operations simple, Act tasks state the required operation explicitly, and Mind2Act tasks chain dependent operations so that each physical outcome decides what comes next. Success is judged from physical predicates on the environment, and the evaluator records stages and events within each episode. Each task has three difficulty levels that raise its demands while keeping the objective fixed. Each level runs in a Clean and a Random scene, which share the same instance but differ in clutter, materials and lighting (180 configurations in total). Agents and end-to-end policies share the same tasks, information contract and evaluator, and 4,500 demonstrations (75.8 hours) are provided for fine-tuning end-to-end policies. A diagnosis harness combines rule-based analysis of the evaluator’s stage and event records with an LLM judge to attribute each failed episode of three representative systems to Mind , Act , or their composition. It summarizes each of these systems in a per-model report called a model profile card (Fig. 5 ; Appendix E.4 ). Our evaluation on Mind2Act World reveals a clear pattern. Existing architectures are uneven across Mind and Act , yet all struggle with Mind-Action Composition . The strongest agent retains task state well but struggles to sustain contact, and its timed successes are measured with a simulator that pauses during inference. End-to-end policies respond within a fraction of a second and execute practiced motions, but retain little task state, and the memory of the VLAs largely disappears under scene randomization. Notably, on Mind2Act , the strongest system succeeds in only 12.0% of episodes, far below its 52.7% on Mind and 39.0% on Act , and no end-to-end policy exceeds 3.6%. Competence in either capability therefore does not carry over to Mind2Act tasks. The contributions of this work are summarized as follows: • We introduce Mind2Act World , a diagnostic benchmark comprising 30 manipulation tasks grounded in real-world requirements. Organized into three views, it systematically evaluates Mind , Act , and Mind-Action Composition . • We develop a diagnosis harness that combines rule-based analysis with an LLM judge to identify the stage at which each failed episode first breaks down and to attribute the failure to Mind , Act , or Mind-Action Composition . The harness also summarizes three representative models in model profile cards of their failure patterns and behavioral tendencies. • We evaluate representative multimodal agents, VLAs, and WAMs on shared tasks and scoring, with separate leaderboards for agents and end-to-end policies. selected.summary: ### Key Features and Enhancements - **Rubin Support (Preview)** - Added preview support for NVIDIA Rubin (SM107), validated on Vera Rubin. - Added DeepSeek-V4 and Kimi K3 support on Vera Rubin. - **Model Support** - Added DeepSeek-V4 support on Blackwell and Rubin (preview). - Added Kimi K3 support on Blackwell and Rubin (preview), including multimodal and multi-node serving. Attention data parallelism (DEP16) requires GB300-class GPU memory. - Added Qwen3.5 support on Hopper, Blackwell and Rubin (preview), including MTP and NVFP4 on Blackwell, and Qwen3.6 and Qwen3.8-Flash-Next support on Blackwell. - Added MiniMax-M3 support on Blackwell and Rubin (preview). - Added GLM-5, GLM-5.2, Kimi-K2.5 and Step-3.7-Flash support on Blackwell. - Added Nemotron Nano Omni support on Hopper and Blackwell. - Added Gemma 4 support on Blackwell, including multimodal. - Added Laguna support on Hopper and Blackwell. - Added prefix caching for Mamba hybrid models, such as Qwen3.5 and Nemotron Super V3. - **Features** - **Performance:** - Optimized DeepSeek-V4, DeepSeek-V3.2, Qwen3.5, Gemma 4, MiniMax-M3 and Kimi K3 with model-specific kernel fusions. - Added locality domain (uGPU) localization for NVFP4 MoE on Rubin, which keeps memory traffic local to each GPU die. It is enabled by default; set `DISABLE_LOCALITY_DOMAINS=1` to disable it. - Reduced host overhead with async preprocessing and sync-free beam search, and reduced startup time with checkpoint read-ahead. - Added cascade attention and low-M BF16 GEMM dispatch for SM10x. - **Disaggregated Serving:** - Added gen-first scheduling, conversation affinity routing, beam search and hybrid model support. - Added disaggregated serving for Qwen3.8-Flash-Next. - **Speculative Decoding:** - Added DSpark, DFlash, Suffix Automaton and PARD drafters. - Added EAGLE3 dynamic trees, Eagle 3.1 draft models and speculative decoding with LoRA. - Added rejection sampling for one-model paths and acceptance-rate-based auto-disable for dynamic speculation. - Added loading MTP weights from standalone checkpoints. - **Parallelism and MoE:** - Added DWDP (Distributed Weight Data Parallelism), extended Helix context parallelism, and a KV cache-aware attention-DP router. - Added the `DENSEGEMM`, `MEGAMOE_DEEPGEMM`, `MEGAMOE_CUTEDSL`, `CUTEDSL_FC12` (Rubin only) and `MARLIN` MoE backends. - Added an NCCL-EP backend and support for up to 2048 experts. - Added Router Replay (`return_routed_experts`) to return per-token MoE routing for RL training. - **KV Cache:** - KV Cache Manager V2 is selected per model and enabled by default for most model families. - Added KV cache compression (TriAttention and NVFP4 cold-page compression), NVFP4 KV cache and disk cache. - Added per-conversation block reuse and exact multimodal KV block hashing. - Added FlexKV and LMCache connectors. - **Quantization:** - Added MXFP8 (W8A8) linear and MoE support, including MXFP8 checkpoints such as MiniMax-M3. - Added W4A16 NVFP4 weight-only quantization through Marlin, so NVFP4 checkpoints run on Hopper and Ada Lovelace. - Added tunable NVFP4 quantization. - Added support for both legacy and ModelOpt 1.x quantization config formats. - **Sparse Attention:** Added DSA FP4/FP8 decode kernels, GVR Top-K, Skip Softmax Attention (with optional 2:4 activation sparsity on Rubin) and MiniMax-M3 MSA. - **Serving and APIs:** - Added the Anthropic Messages API (`/v1/messages`) and extended the Responses API. - Added a gRPC server and multi-process HTTP frontends. - Added per-request `priority` and named-function `tool_choice` to the OpenAI-compatible APIs. - Added `auto` tool and reasoning parser selection, and GLM-4.7, GLM-5 and Laguna tool parsers. - Added Prometheus metrics and `/start_profile` and `/stop_profile` profiling endpoints. - Added `trtllm-serve`
